# trader-alerts

Price Alerts watches the numbers so the user does not have to stare at a
chart. An alert is information, never an order: when a stop alert rings,
nothing is sold by this skill. With a bracket order the stop-loss and the
take-profit already sit at the broker and do the work; the alerts tell the
user what happened and when it is time to be flat.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" clock                          # NYSE open or closed, next open
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --from-plan                # stop, target, flat by close from trader/plan.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --opening-bell
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --symbol TSLA --stop 358.32
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --symbol TSLA --target 370.04
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --at 15:55 --label "flat by close" --before-close
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --symbol KO --pct 3
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" check                          # exit 0 = something rang
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" quote TSLA --write             # -> trader/prices.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" quote --holdings --write       # portfolio + plan tickers
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" list
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" reset tsla-plan-stop
```

`--now "2026-10-19 15:55"` pins the clock (New York time); `--offline DIR`
reads saved quote files instead of the network.

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/plan.json` | the trade from trader-exit, for `add --from-plan` |
| `trader/alerts.json` | the rules (`alerts.example.json` in this folder) |
| `trader/state/alerts.json` | which rules rang and when, so each rings once |
| `trader/prices.json` | the latest quotes, merged in, for trader-budget and trader-risk |
| `trader/portfolio.json` | the tickers held, for `quote --holdings` |

## Rule types

| type | rings when | rings again |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `above` / `target` | price at or above `price` | after `reset`, or on its own if `"rearm": true` and the price fell back |
| `below` / `stop` | price at or below `price` | same |
| `pct_move` | moved `pct` percent from the previous close (or `ref`), optional `direction` up or down | once per day at most |
| `time` | the New York clock passed `at` ("15:55") on a trading day | once per trading day |
| `opening_bell` | the NYSE is open | once per trading day |

A rule with `"date"` is watched on that New York date only; `--from-plan`
rules carry the plan's date, so yesterday's stop never rings today. A `time`
rule with `"before_close": true` moves 3 hours earlier on a 1:00 p.m. early
close, so "flat by close" at 15:55 rings at 12:55 on those days.

## Quotes

- `yahoo` (default): `query2.finance.yahoo.com/v8/finance/chart/<TICKER>`, an
  unofficial free JSON endpoint, one request per ticker, half a second apart.
  On a 429 it waits and tries once more; on a 429 or a 5xx after that it
  tries `query1`. It identifies itself as `day-trader-skill/2.0`.
- `stooq`: `stooq.com/q/l/?s=tsla.us&f=sd2t2ohlcv&h&e=csv`, Stooq's free CSV.
  It answered 404 on 2026-10-13; the parser stays for when it is back.
- Free quotes are unofficial, delayed and can lag. They are fine for alerts
  and for checking a size, not for timing an order. The broker's price is the
  one that fills. Each price in `trader/prices.json` keeps its quote time, and
  trader-risk only uses one under 15 minutes old.
- If both are down, read the price from the broker connector (Alpaca
  `get_stock_snapshot`, IBKR `get_price_snapshot`) and write it into
  `trader/prices.json` as `{"as_of": "...Z", "prices": {"TSLA": 366.48}}`.

## The NYSE clock

Regular session 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. New York time, closed on weekends and
on these holidays, from nyse.com/markets/hours-calendars (read 2026-10-13):

- 2026: Jan 1, Jan 19, Feb 16, Apr 3 (Good Friday), May 25, Jun 19, Jul 3
  (Independence Day observed), Sep 7, Nov 26, Dec 25. Early close 1:00 p.m. on
  Nov 27 and Dec 24.
- 2027: Jan 1, Jan 18, Feb 15, Mar 26 (Good Friday), May 31, Jun 18
  (Juneteenth observed), Jul 5 (Independence Day observed), Sep 6, Nov 25,
  Dec 24 (Christmas observed). Early close 1:00 p.m. on Nov 26.

Daylight saving time is worked out in the tool, so it needs no time zone
files and ignores the computer's own zone. For any other year it says the
holiday list is unknown.

## Steps

1. Right after trader-exit writes the plan, run `add --from-plan`. Confirm
   the three alerts back to the user: the stop, the target and the flat-by time.
2. Run `check` while the trade is open: every few minutes from a Claude
   scheduled task or `/loop`. Each run fetches only the tickers in today's
   rules and rings each alert once. A check reads the latest delayed quote;
   it is not a live feed, and a price can pass a level between two checks.
3. Tell the user what rang in one line each. A stop or target alert means the
   bracket order has probably filled: check `get_open_position` and record the
   fill with trader-broker. "Flat by close" means close anything still open:
   trader-broker `flatten`, then trader-risk, then the user's yes. Never act
   for them.

## Example: the reel

TSLA on Monday 2026-10-19: entry 364.18 at 10:15 AM, stop 358.32, target
370.04, flat by 15:55. `add --from-plan` writes `tsla-plan-stop`,
`tsla-plan-target` and `tsla-flat-by` for that day. A `check` at 10:53 reads
the real 10:52 quote, 366.48, between the stop and the target:

```
NYSE OPEN (2026-10-19 10:53 New York, regular session).
Nothing hit. 3 rule(s) watched today, TSLA $366.48.
```

At 3:55 PM:

```
ALERT Flat by close: it is 15:55 New York (set for 15:55), the market closes at 16:00. If TSLA is still
open, close it: trader-broker flatten --symbol TSLA builds the sell ticket, then trader-risk and your yes.
```

It rings once. The next morning the plan's three alerts are no longer
watched; with `add --opening-bell`, the bell rings at 9:30.

## Rules

- An alert is a fact about a price or the clock. Say it as a fact.
- Never present a quote as live. Free quotes are delayed and unofficial.
- Confirm every new rule back to the user: ticker, type, level, day.

## What it never does

It never places, cancels or changes an order, never claims a quote is
live, and never predicts where a price is going.

# trader-analyst

Earnings move stocks more than anything else on the calendar, and the press
release is written to put the best number first. This skill reads the numbers
the company actually filed with the SEC, lines them up quarter by quarter, and
says plainly what changed. For a day trader it answers two questions before a
trade: what did the last report say, and is the next one inside this trade?

Tool in this folder (standard library Python, no keys):

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/facts.py" --help
```

It needs the SEC User-Agent (`sec_user_agent` in `trader/config.json`, or
`SEC_USER_AGENT`): "Your Name you@example.com" with the user's real name and
email. It refuses to call SEC without one.

## What it reads and writes

- Reads `https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK##########.json` (every
  number the company has tagged in its filings), the company's submissions
  list (for the newest 10-Q or 10-K and the newest 8-K with item 2.02,
  "Results of Operations") and that 8-K's folder to find the press release
  (the EX-99.1 exhibit).
- Writes `trader/metrics.json` with `--metrics`: one row per company (TTM
  revenue, net income and diluted EPS, the latest margins and growth), for
  your notes or a spreadsheet. `metrics.example.json` in this folder is a
  real run for AAPL, AXP, GOOGL, KO and BAC on 2026-10-13.
- Earnings calls: the tool does not fetch transcripts. If the user pastes one
  (or the company's IR page has it), read it and sum up what management said
  changed: guidance, margins, demand, anything they declined to answer.
- The next report date is not in SEC data. Look for it in `/trader-news`
  headlines or on the company's investor relations page, and say where it
  came from.

## The rules

- **Filed numbers first.** The table comes from XBRL facts the company filed.
  Use the press release for context (guidance, segment colour), and say which
  numbers came from where.
- **Compare like with like.** Growth is against the same quarter a year
  earlier. Quarter-on-quarter changes are shown but many businesses are
  seasonal (Apple's December quarter is always its biggest).
- **Say what is derived.** Companies do not file a Q4 10-Q. The fourth
  quarter is the 10-K year minus the three quarters inside it and is marked
  "derived"; derived EPS is approximate.
- **Say when the data lags.** SEC's facts API can trail a filing. When the
  newest 10-Q is later than the newest quarter in the facts, the tool prints a
  NOTE with the link: read the 10-Q itself before summarising.
- **Flag one-offs.** When net income is above operating income, gains outside
  the business (investment marks, tax items) are inside it. The tool says so.
  Banks and insurers have no gross margin: blank, not zero.

## Steps

1. Run it for the companies in question (or the tickers on
   `trader/watchlist.json`):

   ```bash
   python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/facts.py" TSLA
   python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/facts.py" TSLA NVDA AMD --metrics trader/metrics.json
   ```

   `--quarters 8` shows two years, `--json` everything machine-readable,
   `--cik` a company without a ticker.
2. Open the latest earnings press release (the EX-99 link) and the 10-Q when
   the numbers need context, and read them.
3. Write the summary: one line on the quarter (revenue, EPS, growth), one on
   margins, one on anything unusual (a one-off, a derived quarter, data that
   lags), and the links. Plain words, real numbers, no adjectives the numbers
   do not support.
4. If the next report falls inside the planned trade (an overnight hold, or a
   report before the open), say it before `/trader-exit` sets the stop: a stop
   does not protect against a gap, the stock can open past it.

## Example: the reel's stock

`facts.py TSLA` (run 2026-10-20): quarter ending 2026-06-30 (Q2 2026),
revenue $28.24B, +25.5% against a year earlier, net income $1.11B (-4.9%),
diluted EPS $0.32 (-3.0%); gross margin 16.8% (-4.3 points on the quarter
before), operating margin 1.4%; last four quarters $103.6B revenue and $1.08
EPS. The tool flags that net income is above operating income, so gains
outside the business are inside it. Latest 10-Q filed 2026-07-23. Monday's
headlines said Tesla reports this week, so the summary ends: "The next report
is days away. A day trade that closes before the bell is not exposed to it;
anything held overnight is."

`facts.py AAPL` (2026-10-13): revenue $109.42B, +16.4% against a year
earlier, diluted EPS $2.02 (+28.7%). For Coca-Cola the tool noted that SEC's
facts stopped at 2026-04-03 while the 10-Q for 2026-07-03 was already filed,
so the summary read that 10-Q directly.

## What it never does

- Never says a stock is cheap, expensive, a buy or a sell. It reports what
  the company filed.
- Never invents a number the filings do not have, or estimates a quarter it
  cannot derive.
- Never calls SEC without the User-Agent, and stays well under 10 requests a
  second.

## Safety

Education and tooling, not financial advice. This skill only reads filings.
Nothing places an order except `/trader-broker`, after `/trader-risk` passes
and the user types an explicit yes for that order.

# trader-broker

The Order Executor is the only skill in this pack that can lead to a real
order, so it is the strictest. An order reaches the market only after three
separate gates, every time, for every order:

1. **trader-risk passed this exact order today** (matched by fingerprint).
2. **The user typed an explicit yes for this one order** in the chat.
3. **The user clicked Allow once** on Claude's own permission card, which
   appears because the order tool is set to "Needs approval".

Two yeses from the user, one PASS from the rules. No yes, no order.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" show                     # every ticket, READY or not
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" approve --index 1 --reply "yes"
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" result --index 1 --status placed --broker-id ID --filled-qty 8 --filled-price 364.20
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" fill --symbol TSLA --side sell --qty 8 --price 370.04
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" flatten --symbol TSLA --qty 8
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" log
```

`ticket.py` never talks to a broker. It renders tickets, checks that a reply
is a real yes for that order, builds the flatten ticket, and keeps the log in
`trader/state/broker.json`. `--now "2026-10-19 10:15"` pins the clock (New York time).

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/orders.json` | the proposed orders (trader-budget writes it; `flatten` replaces it) |
| `trader/state/risk.json` | trader-risk's verdicts; only a PASS from today is READY |
| `trader/state/broker.json` | every yes, no, placed, failed and filled, with each entry's max loss |
| `trader/portfolio.json` | cash and shares, updated by `fill` and by `result --filled-qty` |
| `trader/plan.json` | the flat-by time for `flatten` |

## Setup A: Alpaca (official MCP server, Claude Desktop)

Alpaca's own server is github.com/alpacahq/alpaca-mcp-server (MIT). It runs on
the user's computer inside Claude Desktop. It is not in Claude's connector
directory. It trades on a **paper** account unless told otherwise. Checked
against its source on 2026-10-20 (version 2.4.0).

1. The user makes an Alpaca account and creates **paper trading** API keys in
   the Alpaca dashboard. Paper keys are separate from live keys.
2. The user installs `uv` (it provides `uvx`), from docs.astral.sh/uv.
3. In Claude Desktop: Settings > Developer > Edit Config. That opens
   `claude_desktop_config.json` (macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/`,
   Windows: `%APPDATA%\Claude\`). The user adds this block (also in
   `claude_desktop_config.example.json` here) and types their own keys into the file:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "alpaca": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["alpaca-mcp-server"],
      "env": {
        "ALPACA_API_KEY": "paste your paper key here, in this file only",
        "ALPACA_SECRET_KEY": "paste your paper secret here, in this file only",
        "ALPACA_PAPER_TRADE": "true",
        "ALPACA_TOOLSETS": "account,trading,stock-data"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

   The `env` block hands the keys to the server as environment variables.
   **Keys never go in the chat.** Never ask for them, never read this file
   back into the conversation, and if the user pastes a key anyway, tell them
   to delete that message and make new keys in the Alpaca dashboard.
   `ALPACA_PAPER_TRADE` is already true by default; writing it makes it
   visible. `ALPACA_TOOLSETS` is optional and hides the tools they do not need.
4. Restart Claude Desktop.
5. **Set the tool permissions.** Customize > Connectors (Settings > Connectors
   in older versions), open alpaca, and for each tool pick Always allow, Needs
   approval or Blocked:
   - `place_stock_order`: **Needs approval**. Never Always allow.
   - every other tool that places, changes, cancels or closes anything
     (`cancel_order_by_id`, `replace_order_by_id`, `close_position`,
     `update_account_config`): Needs approval.
   - `place_option_order`, `place_crypto_order`, `close_all_positions`,
     `cancel_all_orders`, `exercise_options_position`,
     `do_not_exercise_options_position`: **Blocked** unless the user has a
     reason and says so.
   - read-only tools (`get_account_info`, `get_all_positions`, `get_open_position`,
     `get_orders`, `get_clock`, `get_stock_snapshot`, `get_stock_latest_quote`):
     Always allow is fine.
6. Check it: ask Claude for the Alpaca account info (read only) and confirm
   in the Alpaca dashboard that it is the paper account.

In Claude Code instead of Claude Desktop, keep the order tool on ask in
`.claude/settings.json`: `"permissions": {"ask": ["mcp__alpaca__place_stock_order"]}`,
and never put an order tool in `allow`.

**Bracket orders on Alpaca.** `place_stock_order` takes
`take_profit_limit_price` and `stop_loss_stop_price` (and an optional
`stop_loss_limit_price`). When either is there, the server sets
`order_class` to "bracket" by itself; trader-budget writes it anyway so the
ticket shows it. A bracket is whole shares only, with `time_in_force` day or

# trader-budget

The Budget Manager turns a plan ("buy TSLA at 364.18, stop 358.32") into an
exact order ("buy 8 shares"), inside rules the user sets once. The stop
decides the size: the further away the stop, the fewer shares. It writes a
proposal only. trader-risk checks it and trader-broker asks the user yes or
no. Day trading loses most people money. Sizing to a max loss keeps each
loss small; it does not make a trade win.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py"                        # trader/plan.json + trader/config.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py" --write                # write trader/orders.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py" --limit --write        # a limit order at the plan's entry
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py" --limit 364.00 --json  # a limit order at 364.00
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py" --weights AAPL=40,KO=60 --config split.json   # weights mode, below
```

`--now "2026-10-19 10:15"` pins the clock (New York time). A plan for
another day is refused: make a new one with trader-exit.

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/config.json` | the rules (start from `config.example.json` in this folder) |
| `trader/plan.json` | the trade: entry, stop, target, setup, flat-by time (trader-exit writes it) |
| `trader/prices.json` | optional: a fresh price above the plan's entry means a bigger risk (trader-alerts writes it) |
| `trader/portfolio.json` | optional: its cash caps the size (trader-broker keeps it) |
| `trader/orders.json` | the one proposed bracket order it writes with `--write` |

## Step 1: set the rules once

If `trader/config.json` does not exist, copy `config.example.json` into
`trader/config.json` and ask the user for each value in plain words:

- **budget**: how much money this is for. Only money they can afford to lose.
- **cash_buffer_pct**: how much always stays in cash (default 10).
- **max_loss_per_trade_usd**: the most one trade may lose if the stop fills at the stop (default 50).
- **max_position_pct**, **max_order_usd**, **min_order_usd**: the biggest position (75% of the
  budget), the biggest order ($4,000) and the smallest order ($5).
- The day limits trader-risk enforces: **max_daily_loss_usd** (150), **max_trades_per_day** (3),
  **min_reward_risk** (1.0), **require_stop** (true), **no_entries_before** / **no_entries_after**
  ("09:45" / "15:30") and **flat_by** ("15:55"), all New York time.
- **blocked**: tickers they never want to trade.
- Keep **paper** true until they have watched it work on a paper account.

## Step 2: size the trade

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py" --write
```

Whole shares only: Alpaca takes no fractions in a bracket order. The size is
the smallest of four limits:

| limit | shares |
| --- | --- |
| max loss | `max_loss_per_trade_usd` / risk a share (entry minus stop) |
| position cap | budget x `max_position_pct` / entry |
| max order | `max_order_usd` / entry |
| cash | (budget minus the cash buffer) / entry, never more than the cash in `trader/portfolio.json` |

The entry it sizes at: the limit price with `--limit`. For a market order, the
plan's entry, or the price in `trader/prices.json` if it is fresh (under 15
minutes old) and higher. A price that ran up since the plan means a bigger
loss at the same stop, so fewer shares. A lower price never shrinks the risk.

It refuses, and writes no order, when: the size is zero shares, the order is
under the minimum, reward:risk is under `min_reward_risk`, the stop is not
below the entry, the target is not above it (the move already happened), the
plan is for another day, the ticker is blocked, or the plan is a short. Say
the reason to the user in one line.

## Step 3: show the user

Show the four limits, which one decided the size, the shares, the dollars
and the max loss at the stop. Say plainly that a stop is an order, not a
promise: in a fast market it can fill below the stop. Then hand over to
`/trader-risk`.

## Example: the reel

TSLA on Monday 2026-10-19. Opening-range breakout: entry 364.18 at 10:15 AM,
stop 358.32 (the opening-range midpoint), target 370.04 (1R). Risk 5.86 a
share. The example config: $5,000 budget, 10% cash buffer, $50 max loss.

| limit | the math | shares |
| --- | --- | --- |
| max loss | $50 / 5.86 | **8 (decides it)** |
| position cap | 75% of $5,000 = $3,750 / 364.18 | 10 |
| max order | $4,000 / 364.18 | 10 |
| cash | $5,000 minus $500 = $4,500 / 364.18 | 12 |

8 shares = $2,913.44. Max loss at the stop: 8 x 5.86 = $46.88. It writes:

```json
{"symbol": "TSLA", "side": "buy", "qty": "8", "type": "market", "time_in_force": "day",
 "order_class": "bracket", "take_profit_limit_price": "370.04", "stop_loss_stop_price": "358.32",
 "why": "opening-range breakout on TSLA: 8 shares, bound by your $50 max loss per trade (8 x 5.86 = $46.88 at the stop)",
 "plan": {"entry": 364.18, "stop": 358.32, "target": 370.04, "risk_per_share": 5.86, "max_loss": 46.88,
          "setup": "orb", "entry_time": "10:15 AM", "flat_by": "15:55"}}
```

`why` and `plan` are notes for trader-risk and trader-broker. They are never
sent to Alpaca. With the stop at 300.00 instead, one share would risk 64.18,
more than the $50 max loss: no order. At 10:52 the real quote was 366.48, so
the same plan sizes to 6 shares at 8.16 a share, and reward:risk falls to
0.44: refused, because the move it was waiting for has mostly happened.

## Weights mode (kept from v1)

`--weights AAPL=22.04,KO=10.86` or `--targets FILE` (`targets.example.json`
here) splits a budget across a list by weight: the cash buffer comes off the
top, weights are renormalised to 100, any stock over `max_position_pct` is
pinned at the cap and its excess shared out, slices under the minimum order
are dropped, and amounts round to whole dollars so nothing is left idle by
accident. With `"max_position_pct": 25` and `"fractional": true`, the example
file gives AAPL $1,250 (capped), AXP $1,119, GOOGL $823, KO $708, BAC $600.
With `"fractional": false` (the example config) it buys whole shares and
needs prices (`--prices trader/prices.json`). These are plain buys with no stop: trader-risk blocks them while
`require_stop` is true and counts each one against `max_trades_per_day`. Use
a separate config (`--config`) for a long-term split.

## Rules

- Proposals only. This skill never calls a broker tool.
- Never size money the user has not said is for this. Ask for the budget and the max loss.
- Every number comes from the config, the plan or the prices. Nothing is guessed.
- No projections: never say what a trade will make. A target is a plan, not a forecast.
- Free Yahoo prices are unofficial and can lag. The broker's price is the one that fills.

It never places, approves or schedules an order, never raises a limit on its
own, never shrinks a stop to fit more shares, and never sizes options,
margin or short positions.

argument-hint: "[TICKER] [--setup orb|level] [--interval 5m|1m]"

# trader-entry

The Entry Timer turns a setup into one moment: the bar that confirms it. It
reads bars, 1-minute or 5-minute, and waits for each one to finish. A price
that pokes above the high in the middle of a bar is not an entry. A bar that
CLOSES above it is. Then it says the time and the price, writes them down for
the Exit Planner, and stops. It never buys anything. Day trading loses most
people money, and a clean signal does not change that.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/entry.py" check TSLA                  # 15-minute opening range, 5-minute bars
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/entry.py" check TSLA --write          # also save trader/entry.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/entry.py" check TSLA --setup level --level 371.20
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/entry.py" check TSLA --interval 1m --min-volume-x 1.5
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/entry.py" watch TSLA --until 15:30    # one line per closed bar, stops on the trigger
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/entry.py" watchlist                   # every hit in trader/watchlist.json
```

Other flags: `--or-minutes N` (default 15), `--json`, `--offline FILE` (a
saved Yahoo chart JSON, `.json` or `.json.gz`, or a folder of
`<TICKER>.json`), `--now "2026-10-19 10:15"` (New York time) to replay a day.
`watch` with `--now` or `--offline` runs on a simulated clock and replays the
day bar by bar without waiting.

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/watchlist.json` | the scanner's hits (`hits[].symbol`), for `watchlist` |
| `trader/config.json` | `no_entries_before` (09:45) and `no_entries_after` (15:30), New York time. Optional |
| Yahoo chart API | today's bars, `range=1d&interval=5m` (or `1m`): free, unofficial, can lag |
| `trader/entry.json` | with `check --write`, or when `watch` triggers: symbol, setup, status, time, bar, price, level, opening range |

## The rule

- **Opening range (orb).** The high and low of the first 15 minutes: the
  9:30, 9:35 and 9:40 five-minute bars, or fifteen 1-minute bars. The level
  to beat is the range high.
- **Level.** A price you give, like a 20-day high from `/trader-scanner`.
- **The trigger** is the first completed bar after the range that CLOSES
  above the level. A wick above is not a trigger. A close exactly at the
  level is not above it.
- **The time** is that bar's close time (the 10:10 bar closes at 10:15 AM).
  The price is its close, to the cent.
- **Only closed bars count.** A bar is closed when the clock passes its start
  plus 5 (or 1) minutes and Yahoo has caught up to that moment (it waits a
  minute at most). Yahoo's live tick, like 10:49:45, is never a bar.
- **Volume, if you want it.** `--min-volume-x 1.5` also needs the trigger
  bar's volume at 1.5 times the range bars' average. The 9:30 bar holds the
  opening auction, so 1.0 is already strict.
- **Time limits.** No entries before 9:45 or after 15:30 (config). On a 1:00
  p.m. early close the cutoff moves up with the close, to 12:30.
- **What it says.** Waiting (and how far the last close is from the level),
  triggered, expired, or no data. Before 9:30: not open yet. Before 9:45: the
  range is still forming. Weekends and NYSE holidays: the market is closed.

## Steps

1. Get the symbol from the user, or run `entry.py watchlist` after
   `/trader-scanner`. Check `/trader-news` for it first.
2. Run `entry.py check SYMBOL`. Tell the user the status in one line:
   waiting and how far, triggered at what time and price, or expired.
3. To wait for it, Claude can run `entry.py watch SYMBOL --until 15:30` in
   the background, or `entry.py check SYMBOL --write` on a `/loop` every 5
   minutes. `watch` wakes just after each bar closes, prints one line per
   bar, and exits 0 on the trigger (it writes `trader/entry.json`) or 1 when
   the setup expires. Keep the computer awake while it watches: a sleeping
   laptop pauses it, and it catches up, late, when it wakes.
4. When it triggers, say the time and the price, and that nothing was placed.
   If the trigger is more than a bar old, say that too: a late entry is a
   different trade.
5. Hand off to `/trader-exit` to set the stop and the target BEFORE anything
   is bought.

## Example: the reel

TSLA, Monday 2026-10-19, 5-minute bars. The opening range is 354.47 to
362.18. At 10:12 the 10:10 bar is still open, so it waits:

```
WAITING  last close $361.68 (10:05 bar), $0.50 under the range high $362.18 (-0.14%).
The 10:10 bar is still forming ($364.18 so far, closes 10:15 AM); it does not count until it closes.
```

At 10:15 the bar has closed:

```
TSLA  Mon 2026-10-19 10:15 ET  opening-range breakout (15-minute range) on 5-minute bars (Yahoo, free, can lag)
Opening range 9:30-9:45: high $362.18, low $354.47 (3 of 3 bars).
TRIGGERED 10:15 AM at $364.18: the 10:10 bar (bar 8) closed above the range high $362.18 (+0.55%).
This is the moment to get in, if you take the trade. Nothing was placed.
Next: set the stop and target BEFORE you buy: /trader-exit (exit.py plan --from trader/entry.json).
```

With `--min-volume-x 1` the 10:10 bar is too thin (0.60x the range's volume)
and the trigger moves to 10:35 AM at 365.75 (the 10:30 bar, 7.98x).

## Rules

- Bar by bar, on free Yahoo 1-minute or 5-minute bars. They are unofficial

# trader-exit

The Exit Planner decides how a trade ends before it starts. The stop is where
the setup has failed. The target is where you take what you came for. Both
are set BEFORE the entry, written down and handed on, so nobody has to decide
anything in the middle of a fast move. A stop is a plan, not a guarantee: a
gap or a fast market can fill past it. Day trading loses most people money,
and a neat plan does not change that.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/exit.py" plan                          # trader/entry.json: midpoint stop, 2R target
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/exit.py" plan --stop or-mid --target 1R --write
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/exit.py" plan --stop atr:1.5           # needs the session's bars (Yahoo or --offline)
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/exit.py" plan --symbol TSLA --entry 364.18 --or-high 362.18 --or-low 354.47
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/exit.py" show                          # the current trader/plan.json
```

Other flags: `--flat-by 15:55`, `--json`, `--now "2026-10-19 10:15"` (New
York time), `--entry PRICE` with a waiting entry.json to plan ahead, `--setup
level`, `--offline FILE` (a saved Yahoo chart JSON for an ATR stop).

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/entry.json` | the trigger from trader-entry: symbol, entry price, time, bar, opening range |
| `trader/config.json` | `flat_by` (15:55) and `min_reward_risk` (1.0: a note here, trader-risk enforces it) |
| Yahoo chart API | only for an `atr:K` stop: the session's bars up to the entry bar, free and unofficial |
| `trader/plan.json` | with `--write`: entry, stop and its rule, target and its R, risk a share, reward:risk, flat by. trader-timemachine, trader-budget and trader-alerts read it |

## Stops and targets

| stop | where it goes |
| --- | --- |
| `or-mid` | the opening-range midpoint (the default for an opening-range breakout) |
| `or-low` | the opening-range low: wider, so fewer shares for the same max loss |
| `price:X` | your price |
| `pct:X` | X percent under the entry |
| `atr:K` | K times the 14-bar ATR under the entry, on the session's bars up to the entry bar. With fewer than 14 bars by then it averages all of them and says so |

A level setup has no opening range to lean on, so it needs a stop you name.

- **Rounding.** The stop rounds AWAY from the entry to the cent (down, for a
  long). Risk = entry minus stop. Target = entry + R x risk, rounded half up
  to the cent. `2R` by default; `1R`, `1.5R` or `price:X` also work.
- **Refused, with the reason.** A stop at or above the entry. A target at or
  below it. A risk under 0.05% of the price: too tight to survive the
  spread, normal wiggle would stop you out. An entry.json that has not
  triggered (unless you give `--entry`). A short: v2 plans longs only.
- **Flat by.** 15:55 by default (or `flat_by` in the config). Out by then,
  win or lose, no overnight hold. On a 1:00 p.m. early close it moves up to
  12:55. An entry at or after the flat-by time is refused.

## Steps

1. Run it right after `/trader-entry` triggers. Before that, `--entry PRICE`
   plans ahead at the level you expect.
2. Use the default stop for an opening-range breakout unless the user names
   another. A level setup needs one: ask.
3. Run `exit.py plan --write`. Read back the entry, the stop and its rule,
   the target and its rule, the risk a share, reward:risk and flat by.
4. If it refuses, say the reason and the fix (a wider stop, a farther
   target). Never loosen anything on your own.
5. Say once that the stop is a plan, not a guarantee.
6. Hand off to `/trader-timemachine` to replay the plan, then `/trader-budget`
   to size it to the max loss per trade. Offer `/trader-alerts` for the stop,
   the target and the flat-by time. Claude can keep `entry.py watch` running
   in the background or on a `/loop` until a setup triggers, then come here.

## Example: the reel

TSLA, Monday 2026-10-19. The entry is 364.18 at 10:15 AM (the 10:10 bar,
bar 8) and the opening range is 354.47 to 362.18. `exit.py plan --stop
or-mid --target 1R --write`:

```
Exit plan: TSLA long, Mon 2026-10-19, opening-range breakout on 5-minute bars
  Entry         $364.18 at 10:15 AM (bar 8)
  Stop          $358.32  opening-range midpoint: ($362.18 + $354.47) / 2 = $358.325, rounded down
  Target        $370.04  1R (one times the risk)
  Risk a share  $5.86 (1.61% of the entry)
  Reward:risk   1.0
  Flat by       15:55 ET, win or lose: no overnight hold
```

The default 2R target would be 364.18 + 2 x 5.86 = 375.90. trader-budget then
sizes it: a $50 max loss per trade buys floor(50 / 5.86) = 8 shares.

## Rules

- The stop and the target are set before the entry, never after.
- Never move a stop further from the entry once the trade is on.
- Plain numbers only: entry, stop, target, risk a share, reward:risk. It
  never prints a P&L or a return.
- Nothing here promises winning trades or money. A 1R target is not a
  prediction that the price gets there.
- Long side only. v2 plans longs only.

## What it never does

It never places an order, never sizes a position, never widens a stop to
make a plan pass, and never calls a stop a guarantee.

## Safety

# trader-news

A chart can look perfect and still be about to gap on an earnings date, a
halt or a lawsuit. Before a setup becomes a trade, this skill reads the two
feeds that carry those first, for every stock on the watchlist, and tells you
only what is new. It also prints how far each stock has moved today, so a
headline and a move sit side by side.

Tool in this folder (standard library Python, no keys):

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/news.py"                         # watchlist + plan + portfolio
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/news.py" --tickers TSLA NVDA --hours 12
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/news.py" --no-sec --json
```

## What it reads and writes

| file / feed | what |
| --- | --- |
| `--tickers`, else `trader/watchlist.json` | the scanner's hits (trader-scanner) |
| `trader/plan.json` | the trade you are planning (trader-exit) |
| `trader/portfolio.json` | what you hold (trader-broker records fills there) |
| Yahoo Finance headline RSS | `https://feeds.finance.yahoo.com/rss/2.0/headline?s=TSLA&region=US&lang=en-US` |
| Yahoo Finance chart endpoint | the last price against yesterday's close (unofficial, can lag) |
| SEC EDGAR company Atom feed | 8-K by default (`--forms 8-K,10-Q` for more); needs `sec_user_agent` in `trader/config.json` or `SEC_USER_AGENT`, else filings are skipped with a note |
| `trader/state/news.json` | what has been shown (kept 30 days) and each ticker's CIK |

## The rules

- **Headlines are leads, not facts.** Before telling the user something
  happened, open the story or the filing and read it. Quote the source and
  link it. Never summarise a paywalled story you could not read: say so.
- **Filings beat headlines.** If an 8-K and a headline disagree, the 8-K is
  what the company told the SEC.
- **Say what it touches.** Every item lists the tickers it touches and its
  tags: earnings, analyst, legal, deal, capital, people, risk, halt,
  regulatory, macro. Filings marked `!` carry an important 8-K item: earnings
  results (2.02), an officer change (5.02), an impairment (2.06), a delisting
  notice (3.01), past financials no longer reliable (4.02), bankruptcy (1.03)
  or a cyber incident (1.05).
- **MOVING** marks a stock 3 % or more from yesterday's close (`--move-pct`).
  A move with no headline is worth saying out loud too.
- **No predictions.** Report what was published and how far the price is from
  yesterday's close. Never say what the stock will do next.

## Steps

1. Run the check: `python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/news.py"`. Exit code 1 means
   nothing new. `--all` shows items already seen, `--json` gives everything
   machine readable, `--dry-run` leaves the state alone.
2. Read the items that matter: every `!` filing, anything tagged earnings,
   halt, legal, regulatory or risk, and every MOVING ticker first.
3. Write a short brief, per ticker: what happened, the source and link, the
   move, and one line on why it matters to the setup (for example "earnings
   are this week: an overnight gap can jump past any stop").
4. If a story changes the picture, say so before `/trader-entry` and
   `/trader-exit`: an earnings date inside the trade, a halt, an offering.
   Never act on a headline alone.

During the session: `/loop 15m /trader-news`, or a scheduled task each
morning before the open.

## Example: the reel

Monday 2026-10-19, TSLA broke its opening range at 10:15 AM ET. The check at
10:15 (Yahoo Finance's TSLA feed, 16 headlines since 8:00) leads with the
morning's real stories: "Meta and Musk earnings and September pending home
sales: What to Watch" (8:00, earnings), "Tesla-SpaceX Merger Mania Strikes
Wall Street Ahead of Earnings" (8:04, earnings, deal), "Tech Stock Rebound
Nudges US Equity Futures Mostly Higher Pre-Bell" (8:02, macro). The brief:
"Tesla reports this week, so the stock can gap overnight; today's trade is
in and out before the close. No new 8-K." At 10:52 the price line reads
`TSLA 366.48 +3.31% vs yesterday's close 354.72 at 10:52 ET  MOVING`. When a
ticker has no news, say so rather than padding the brief.

## What it never does

- Never invents or embellishes a story, a quote or a number.
- Never trades on news, and never tells the user to buy or sell because of a
  headline.
- Never hammers a server: one request per feed per ticker, a pause between
  calls, and SEC's 10 requests a second limit stays far away.

## Safety

Education and tooling, not financial advice. This skill only reads and
reports. Nothing places an order except `/trader-broker`, after
`/trader-risk` passes and the user types an explicit yes for that order.

# trader-pelosi

Members of Congress have to report their trades, their spouse's and their
dependent children's. The House Clerk posts every report as a PDF and lists
them all in one index file per year. This skill reads that index, notices the
moment a new report appears, and reads the report for you.

It is fast. It is not early. A PTR is due within 30 days of the member
learning of the trade and never more than 45 days after it, so by the time
anyone can read it the trade is days or weeks old. There is no inside
information here: only public filings, read quickly. Say that every time.

Tool in this folder (standard library Python; `pdftotext` from poppler is
optional, to read the PDFs locally):

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" --help
```

## What it reads and writes

- Reads `https://disclosures-clerk.house.gov/public_disc/financial-pdfs/<YEAR>FD.zip`
  (one `<Member>` per filing: name, district, FilingType, FilingDate, DocID)
  and each PTR at `.../public_disc/ptr-pdfs/<YEAR>/<DocID>.pdf`.
- Writes `trader/state/pelosi.json` (the DocIDs already shown, so each PTR
  alerts once) and keeps downloaded PDFs in `trader/state/ptr-pdfs/`.
- Reads `trader/portfolio.json` (if it exists) to flag trades in what you hold.

## The rules

- **Quote the filing, not a tracker.** Every row comes from the PTR PDF on the
  Clerk's site, with its DocID and link. Third-party trackers are fine for
  browsing but can be off (Capitol Trades showed Pelosi's trade dates one day
  earlier than her PTRs). The PTR wins.
- **Amounts are ranges.** "$1,000,001 - $5,000,000", never "$3 million".
- **Owner matters.** SP is the spouse, JT joint, DC a dependent child, blank
  the member. Pelosi's 2026 trades are all SP: Paul Pelosi.
- **Say the delay.** Each row shows how many days passed between the trade
  and the filing; over 45 is flagged as late.
- **Options are options.** A call bought with a strike and an expiry is not
  a share purchase. The tool reads contracts, strike and expiry from the
  description and marks exercises.

## Step 1: what has been filed

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" index --member pelosi
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" index --since 2026-10-01        # every member
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" index --member "Josh Gottheimer" --year 2025
```

`--member` takes a last name, "First Last" or "Last, First", and repeats.
`--type ''` lists every filing type (annual reports are type O).

## Step 2: watch for new ones

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" new --member pelosi --read
```

Shows only PTRs not seen at the last check (the first run shows the last 45
days), downloads and reads them with `--read`, and records them in the state
file. Exit code 1 means nothing new. In January it also checks last year's
index. The Clerk rebuilds the index file about once a day (the copy read on
2026-10-13 was stamped 09:00 that morning), so checking every hour on weekdays
is plenty: run it with `/loop 1h` or a scheduled task.

## Step 3: read a report

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" fetch 20035143
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" parse ptr.txt --filed 2026-08-21 --json
```

`fetch` saves the PDF and, if `pdftotext` is installed, prints the rows. If it
is not installed, open the saved PDF and read it directly: you can read PDFs.
`parse` turns `pdftotext -layout` text into rows. Check the row count against
the PDF when a report runs over several pages.

## Example: a real alert

```
NEW Periodic Transaction Report: Hon. Nancy Pelosi (CA11) filed 2026-08-21, doc 20035143
  - spouse purchase, Bloom Energy Corporation Class A Common Stock (BE): 100 call
    options, $100 strike, expires 2027-06-17, $1,000,001 - $5,000,000, traded
    2026-07-24, disclosed 28 days later
```

The same PTR also shows 10,000 and 5,000 BE shares, a second block of 100 BE
calls on 07/28, Intel shares and 50 Intel calls ($50 strike, 6/17/27), and a
private real estate LLC with no ticker. Her other 2026 PTRs: 20033725
(01/23), 20034836 (06/23, Intel and Uber calls) and 20035553 (10/02, a real
estate LLC). Then: "This is a public disclosure filed 28 days after the trade.
It says what Paul Pelosi bought in July, not what anyone will buy next."

If the user wants to act on it, it goes the long way: a disclosure is weeks
old, so it is a reason to look at a chart, not a setup. `/trader-scanner`
and `/trader-entry` decide if there is a trade today; then shares only (the
config has `allow_options: false`), sized by `/trader-budget`, checked by
`/trader-risk`, placed by `/trader-broker` only after their yes.

## The Senate: the manual route

Senate reports live at `https://efdsearch.senate.gov`. Before searching, the
site asks you to tick a box agreeing to the legal limits on how the reports
may be used. That is an agreement for the person to accept, so this skill
does not click it or automate it. The route:

1. The user opens `https://efdsearch.senate.gov/search/` in their browser and
   accepts the agreement themselves.
2. They pick the report type "Periodic Transactions", type the senator's last
   name, set the date range and search.
3. They open the report: electronic filings show a table of transactions,
   paper filings are scanned images.
4. They paste the table (or a screenshot, or the saved page) into the chat,
   and you write it up in the same shape as the House rows, with the report
   link, and the same 45-day caveat.

## What it never does

- Never says or implies a member has inside information, or that copying a
  politician beats the market. No return claims.
- Never presents a range as an exact dollar figure or a tracker's date as the
  trade date.
- Never places an order, and never copies options trades.
- Never automates the Senate agreement or any login.

## Safety

- Education and tooling, not financial advice. Nothing in this pack is a
  recommendation to buy or sell anything.
- Paper trading by default (`"paper": true` in `trader/config.json`).
- Nothing places an order except `/trader-broker`, and only after
  `/trader-risk` passes AND the user types an explicit yes for that order in
  the chat, AND the brokerage tool is set to "Needs approval" in Claude
  (Customize > Connectors > tool permissions) so Claude's own "Allow once /
  Deny" card appears too. Never "Always allow" an order tool.
- No options, margin, shorting or leverage unless the config allows it and
  the user confirms.
- Congressional trades are PUBLIC disclosures filed up to 45 days after the
  trade (STOCK Act). This skill reads them fast; it has no inside
  information, and it says so.

# trader-risk

The Risk Manager is the gate between a proposal and the broker. Every order
written by trader-budget or trader-broker's flatten passes through it. A
BLOCK is final for that order: it does not go to the user for a yes, and it
does not go to the broker. Most people who day trade lose money. These limits
keep each loss and each day's losses small. They do not make a trade win.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/check.py"                           # trader/ files; writes trader/state/risk.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/check.py" --json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/check.py" --no-write                # look without recording
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/check.py" --now "2026-10-19 10:15"  # pin the clock (New York time)
```

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/orders.json` | the proposed orders (trader-budget, or trader-broker's flatten) |
| `trader/config.json` | the limits (trader-budget ships `config.example.json`) |
| `trader/portfolio.json` | cash and holdings; if missing, a fresh account funded with the budget |
| `trader/prices.json` | a fresh price raises the entry it measures risk from; also values holdings |
| `trader/state/broker.json` | what was placed today: duplicates, trades per day, daily loss, day trades |
| `trader/state/risk.json` | the verdicts it writes, with a fingerprint of each exact order |

## Entries and exits

An **entry** opens or adds to a position: a buy, or a sell that would go
short. An **exit** only reduces what you already hold. Getting out must
always be possible, so an exit is checked for format, asset and short sales
only. Every other rule (day limits, entry window, loss, reward:risk, blocked
list, size, duplicates) turns into a warning for an exit, never a BLOCK.

## The checks

Orders are checked in file order, as if each passed order had filled, so a
batch that is fine order by order but breaks a limit together is caught.

| check | blocks when |
| --- | --- |
| format | no symbol, side not buy or sell, both or neither of qty and notional, a notional order that is not market + day (Alpaca's rule), a limit order with no limit price; a bracket that is not whole shares, not `day` or `gtc`, or misses its stop-loss or take-profit |
| asset | an option symbol while `allow_options` is false; crypto or anything that is not a US stock or ETF ticker |
| short | a sell of more than you hold (`allow_short` false) |
| blocked | (entries) the ticker is on the `blocked` list |
| size | (entries) under `min_order_usd` or over `max_order_usd` |
| position | (entries) the stock would be over `max_position_pct` of the account |
| cash | (entries) the buy would leave less than the cash buffer, or need margin |
| stop | (entries) no stop while `require_stop` is true (a bracket `stop_loss_stop_price`, or the order's plan stop); a stop on the wrong side of the entry |
| loss | (entries) qty x (entry minus stop) over `max_loss_per_trade_usd` |
| reward:risk | (entries) (target minus entry) / (entry minus stop) under `min_reward_risk` |
| daily loss | (entries) the max losses at the stops of today's entries, plus this one, over `max_daily_loss_usd` |
| trades | (entries) `max_trades_per_day` entries already placed today |
| window | (entries) before `no_entries_before` or after `no_entries_after`, or the market is closed |
| pdt | (entries, only with `pdt_guard` true) 3 day trades already in the last 5 business days |
| duplicate | (entries) the same symbol and side twice in one batch, or already placed today |
| daily limit | (entries) `max_orders_per_day` orders already placed today |

How the numbers work:

- **The entry it measures from**: the limit price for a limit order. For a
  market order, the HIGHER of the plan's entry and a fresh price from
  `trader/prices.json` (under 15 minutes old). A plan written at 10:15 cannot
  understate the risk at 10:55 after the price ran up. An older price is not
  used, and it says so.
- **Daily loss** counts the full max loss of every entry placed today, win or
  lose, as trader-broker logged it. Three full-size trades use up a $150 day.
- **The window** is New York time, worked out in the tool (daylight saving
  included), never from the computer's clock zone. Weekends and NYSE holidays
  are closed. On a 1:00 p.m. early close the window ends 3 hours earlier too.
  Set both `no_entries_*` to null to switch the window off.
- **pdt_guard** (off by default) counts a day trade as a symbol bought and
  sold on the same day in the log, plus any entry placed today (it is meant
  to be flat by the close). FINRA removed the $25,000 pattern-day-trader
  minimum (Regulatory Notice 26-10, effective June 4, 2026; firms may phase
  in until October 20, 2027), so some brokers still apply the old rule: turn
  `pdt_guard` on if yours does.

Warnings do not block, but say them to the user: a LIVE account, a number
sent as a number instead of a string, a stop that lives only in the plan and
not at the broker, a price too old to use, an early close today.

## Steps

1. If the price may have moved since the plan, refresh it first
   (trader-alerts: `alerts.py quote TSLA --write`).
2. Run `check.py`. Exit code 0 means every order passed, 1 means at least one
   was blocked.
3. Tell the user the result in plain words, order by order: the max loss at
   the stop, reward:risk, and how much of today's limits it uses. For a
   BLOCK, give the reason and the fix (fewer shares, a closer stop from
   trader-exit, wait for the window, or skip the trade). Never change a
   limit yourself.
4. If the order changes in any way, run the check again. trader-broker matches
   each order to its verdict by fingerprint, so an edited order is not ready
   until it passes again, and a verdict from yesterday does not count today.

# trader-scanner

The Chart Scanner is the first step of a day trade. It reads thousands of
free charts and lists the ones that match a rule. That is all it does. A scan
is a list of charts that match a rule, not a list of stocks to buy, and a
setup on a chart is not a prediction. Most people who day trade lose money;
the scanner does not change that. It only saves you from flipping through
5,000 charts by hand.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).


`--or-minutes 15`, `--max-confirm 200` (orb stage 2),
`--now "2026-10-19 10:15"` (New York time) to pin the clock, `--offline PATH`
to read saved Yahoo files, `--no-write`, `--show N`, `--json`. Exit code 0
when the scan found something, 1 when it found nothing or could not run (the
reason is one plain line).

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/universe.txt` | written by `universe`: one `SYMBOL\|Name` a line, read by `daily` and `orb` |
| `trader/watchlist.json` | written by `daily` and `orb`: `mode`, `as_of`, `universe`, `scanned`, `failed`, `hits[]`. trader-news and trader-entry read `hits[].symbol` |
| `trader/config.json` | read by `orb`: `no_entries_after` (default 15:30) |

## The universe

`universe` downloads `nasdaqlisted.txt` and `otherlisted.txt` from
nasdaqtrader.com/dynamic/SymDir and keeps a row when, in this order:

1. It is not a test issue, not an ETF, not NextShares.
2. It is a plain ticker: 1 to 5 letters, or 1 to 4 letters plus one class
   letter after a dot (BRK.B). A `$` preferred (ABR$D) is out, and so is a
   `.U`, `.W` or `.R` suffix (units, warrants, rights).
3. Out, whatever else the name says: warrants; SPAC units and rights ("Units,
   each consisting of", "Rights to receive"); notes, ETNs, debentures; a %
   coupon; "Depositary Shares" that are not American or Global (those carry a
   preferred).
4. In: the name calls it common stock, common shares or units, ordinary
   shares, shares of beneficial interest, ADS / ADR / American or Global
   depositary shares, or partnership or trust units.
5. Out: the name still says unit, right, bond, preferred or preference.
6. In: everything else (plain names like "AMETEK, Inc.").

On the Oct 19 2026 files this keeps 5,943. The reel said 5,259: that count
came from an ad hoc filter (names that say common or ordinary, no ADRs). All
5,259 of those are in this list; the 684 extra are mostly ADRs, closed-end
funds and partnership units. The Oct 20 files gave 5,942.

## The daily scan (before the open)

Yahoo's spark endpoint returns closes for 20 symbols a request, so 5,942
symbols take 298 requests. On Oct 20 2026 that took 145 seconds with the
polite pause (0.3 s). Liquidity comes from the spark meta: last price at
least `--min-price` and last session's volume at least `--min-volume`. Run it
before the open or after the close: during the session the volume is the
day's so far, and today's daily bar is left out until 4:00 PM.

The setups are computed from daily closes only (spark has no highs or lows),
so they are close cousins of the reel's `refs/scan.py`, which used highs and
lows:

| setup | the rule on closes |
| --- | --- |
| `breakout_20d` | the last close is above every close of the 20 sessions before it |
| `bull_flag` | up more than 10 % over the 10 sessions before the last 5, then the last 5 closes inside a 5 % range |
| `reclaim_ma20` | the close before was under its 20-day average, the last close is above it |
| `oversold` | RSI 14 (Wilder) under 30 |
| `oversold_bounce` | RSI 14 was under 30 yesterday and today closed up |

A closing-high breakout fires more often than an intraday-high one (KO on
Oct 16 broke its 20-day closing high, not its 20-day intraday high). Hits are
listed most traded first (price times volume).

## The opening-range breakout scan (during the session)

The opening range is the first `--or-minutes` (15) of the session: the 9:30,
9:35 and 9:40 five-minute bars. A hit is the first completed 5-minute bar
to CLOSE above the range high, at that bar's close time.

1. Stage 1, every symbol: spark closes of today's 5-minute bars, 20 a
   request. A chart goes on only if a completed bar after the range closed at
   or above the highest close of the range. That is a necessary condition
   (the range high is at least every range close), so no breakout is lost.
2. Stage 2, each candidate: the v8 chart with real highs and lows, one
   request each. Range high = the highest high of the range bars, range low =
   the lowest low. On a strong morning most charts are candidates, so stage 2
   checks at most `--max-confirm` (200) of them, the most traded first (price
   times volume so far), and prints PARTIAL with the count it skipped.
   `--max-confirm 0` checks them all.

Timing, live on Tue Oct 20 2026 (a strong morning): 100 liquid names at
10:01 AM took 35 seconds (5 spark requests, 70 v8 charts, 51 of 91 usable
charts broke out). The whole universe at 10:03 AM took about 4 minutes (298
spark requests, then 200 v8 charts): 2,448 usable charts, 1,782 candidates,
the 200 most traded checked, 119 of those broke out. For a fast answer, scan
the daily watchlist or a list of names you trade (`--watchlist`, `--symbols`).

A chart is usable only when every 5-minute bar from 9:30 to the cutoff is
there; a missing bar means a halt or a thin stock. Null closes are dropped,
a bar off the 5-minute grid (the live tick, like 10:58:07) is dropped, and a
bar counts only once it is complete (start + 5 minutes). Before 9:50 AM, on a
weekend or holiday, after the close, or after `no_entries_after` (an expired
setup) it prints one plain line and writes nothing. The 1:00 PM early closes
are in the calendar.

## Data and limits

- Yahoo's chart and spark endpoints are free, unofficial and can lag. Bars are
  5-minute bars, bar by bar, never tick by tick. query2 first, query1 on a 429

- Partial results are said as partial: "Fetched 4,980 of 5,259 charts (279
  failed or had no data)". Never round a partial scan up to "the whole market".
- NYSE holidays and early closes for 2026 and 2027 (nyse.com, read 2026-10-13).

2. Before the open: `scan.py daily`. Tell the user the counts (fetched,

# trader-timemachine

The Time Machine sits between the plan and the money. trader-exit has set
the entry, the stop and the target. Before anything is sized or sent, this
skill asks one question: if today plays out like the stock's own last 60
days, how often does this plan hit the target first, the stop first, or
neither? It answers with 10,000 replays and with the real record of the same
rule on every past session. It is a simulation built from the stock's own
recent bars, not a prediction. Day trading loses most people money, and a
good-looking replay does not change that.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/timemachine.py" run                    # trader/plan.json, 10,000 replays, seed 19
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/timemachine.py" run --write            # also save trader/timemachine.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/timemachine.py" run --until 15:55      # end each replay at your flat-by time
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/timemachine.py" run --json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/timemachine.py" run --symbol TSLA --date 2026-10-19 \
    --entry 364.18 --stop 358.32 --target 370.04 --entry-time "10:15 AM"
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/timemachine.py" chart --from           # ASCII fan chart of the saved run
```

Other flags: `--replays N`, `--seed N` (default 19), `--window N` (default 2
bars), `--offline FILE` (a saved Yahoo chart JSON, `.json` or `.json.gz`),
`--now "2026-10-19 10:15"` (New York time) to pin the clock.

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/plan.json` | the plan from trader-exit: symbol, date, entry, entry_time / entry_bar, stop, stop_rule, target, target_r, opening range |
| Yahoo chart API | one request: 60 days of 5-minute bars (`range=60d&interval=5m`), free and unofficial, can lag |
| `trader/timemachine.json` | with `--write`: `{plan, mc, history}` plus the verdict. `mc` holds the odds, percentiles, the fan-chart bands, 160 sample paths and a 24-bin histogram of the close |

## How it works

1. **The pool.** It keeps only FULL sessions before the plan's date: all 78
   five-minute bars, 9:30 to 4:00 New York time. Half days, gaps and today
   are left out. Every bar becomes four ratios to the bar before it:
   open, high, low and close over the previous close.
2. **One replay.** Start at the entry price. For each bar left in the day,
   pick a past bar from the same time of day (plus or minus 2 bars) at
   random, and scale it to the current price. Bar by bar, it checks the stop
   first, then the target. A bar that touches both counts as the stop.
3. **10,000 replays** give four odds. Target first. Stop first. Neither,
   which means the trade was still open at `--until` (default 4:00 PM, the
   close, or 1:00 PM on an NYSE early-close day). Green, which means target
   first or above the entry at `--until`.
   R is +1 at a 1R target, -1 at the stop, and otherwise the distance from
   the entry at `--until` divided by the risk. A gap through the stop still
   counts as -1R here. A real fill can be worse.
4. **The history.** The plan's own rule (the same opening range, stop rule
   and target R) runs again on every one of those past sessions. That is
   what really happened, not a simulation.
5. **The verdict** is one line from the numbers. It looks only at the
   replays that hit one side, and asks how often the target came first. A
   bigger target needs to win less often to break even: 1 in (1 + R). That
   is 50 % at 1R, 33 % at 2R, 25 % at 3R. Less than 5 points from break-even:
   "Close to a coin flip" at 1R, "Close to break-even" at any other R. 5 to
   15 points: "Leans toward the target" or "Leans toward the stop". 15 or
   more: "Strongly toward" one of them. So a 2R plan with target first
   24.1 % and stop first 50.5 % is close to break-even (it needs 33 % of
   the 74.6 % that hit a side, and got 32 %), not a loser.
6. **Below the verdict**, when it applies: a line when more than 40 % of the
   replays hit neither (the price at `--until` decides those), and the
   average R when its sign goes against the lean. Those can only point the
   other way because of the replays that hit neither.

**The seed.** The draws come from Python's `random.Random(seed)`, seed 19 by
default. Same plan, same data, same seed: the same numbers, on any machine.
Say the seed with every result so the user can repeat it.

**5-minute bars only.** Yahoo keeps 60 days of 5-min bars but only about 7
days of 1-min bars, too few sessions for a fair pool. It refuses, in one
plain line, when there are fewer than 20 full sessions, when the entry bar is
not in the data (wrong date, not closed yet, a future day), or when the plan
does not make sense (a stop above a buy's entry, an entry off the 5-minute
grid). A live in-progress bar is never used.

## Steps

1. Make sure `trader/plan.json` is today's plan from `/trader-exit`. If there
   is none, run that first, or pass the plan as flags.
2. Run `timemachine.py run --write`. Add `--until 15:55` when the plan has a
   flat-by time, so "neither" means still open at the time you would get out.
3. Tell the user, in this order: the four odds, the median and the 5 to 95
   range of the price at the close, the average R, the history line, then the
   verdict line and any line under it exactly as printed. Say the seed.
4. If the verdict is a coin flip or close to break-even, say so plainly. Do
   not dress it up. If the history and the replays disagree, say that too.
5. Say once that this is built from the last 60 days and is not a prediction.
   Earnings, news and halts can do things those 60 days never did. Check
   `/trader-news` for the stock before going on.
6. If the user still wants the trade, hand off to `/trader-budget` to size it.

## Example: the reel

TSLA, Monday 2026-10-19. The 15-minute opening range is 354.47 to 362.18.
The 10:10 bar closes above it: entry 364.18 at 10:15 AM (bar 8), stop 358.32
(the range midpoint, rounded down), target 370.04 (1R, risk 5.86 a share).

```
10,000 replays of the rest of the session, 10:15 AM to 4:00 PM (69 five-minute bars), seed 19.
  target first   29.4 %
  stop first     25.5 %
  neither        45.1 %   still open at 4:00 PM
  green          51.7 %   target first, or above the entry at 4:00 PM
  Price at 4:00 PM: median 364.36, 90 % of replays between 355.54 and 373.54.
  Average R: +0.034
History: the same rule on each of those 59 real sessions fired 33 times:
13 target, 15 stop, 5 neither. Average R -0.062.
Close to a coin flip: target first 29.4 % vs stop first 25.5 %.
45.1 % of the replays hit neither by 4:00 PM; the price at 4:00 PM decides those.
```

At 1R the target has to come first in half of the replays that hit one
side. It did in 53.6 %. The replays came out close to a coin flip, and the
real history was slightly worse than even. That is the honest answer for this setup, and it is what
the user should hear before `/trader-budget` sizes 8 shares.

## Rules

- Every number comes from the run. Never round a coin f
